Well that's the thing, if space is expanding then you'd think matter which is dependent on space would have to be expanding as well.. if space is expanding but matter remains the same size then that'd mean the universe is creating more space but then that'd require a constant source of energy to create it, but if matter is expanding proportionately with space then there'd be no way to tell space is expanding at all because to us it'd appear static.

Can the rate of expansion be affected?

Is there something like "spatial dilation" akin to time dilation as described by the relativity theory?

I think the typical space expansion imagery answers this well enough. Put a few marbles on a balloon. Go blow up the balloon. More precisely the reason we know the universe is expanding is because the distance between everything is increasing and the further away are, the faster they're moving away. If it were somehow just the scale of the universe that was [somehow] increasing, the relative distance between bodies using any sort of relative measurement (which is to say any and all measurements we use) would remain the same.
Nope, this is exactly where the analogy with a balloon fails entirely.

On the large scale of the universe, yes. On the order of galactic superclusters, definitely. On the order of the solar system and the nearest star systems, most likely no. Otherwise, it would be baseless to assert that expansion is occurring at all.
That doesn't make much sense, how can matter be expanding on a large scale but not on the smaller scale? It's all just atoms and subatomic particles anyways

That right there is the question of the century, friend. One explanation attributes this disparity to a cosmological constant, in which gravity is an attractive force nearby, and a repulsive force after a certain distance. Another suggests along your line of thought, that all of spacetime is expanding, but gravity and the other known forces are enough to compensate and keep everything "together", up to a certain distance. Vacuum energy moves along these lines of thought, too.

The forces are something else that don't really make much sense to me. If energy is finite and cannot be created or destroyed then from where do these forces get their seemingly infinite energy to always remaining constant?

It's like magnetism is a switch that doesn't necessarily have to exist but still is constantly on, where is it's energy coming from to always keep it going?

No, it is not. In fact, if all matter was expanding at the same rate as spacetime itself, it would be entirely pointless to say anything is expanding to begin with, since no effect of the expansion would ever be measurable. The place where the common balloon blowing up analogy fails is that gravity, and on smaller scales the other forces, the electromagnetic force and the nuclear forces, keep pulling the matter together to keep its original size. That's why a raisin bread is a better analogy.
Where is this constant source of energy coming from then to create/expand more and more space?

It doesn't require energy to keep expanding, it would require energy to stop the expansion. That would be the very simple explanation if the universe kept on expanding at a constant rate: simple inertia. However, the rate of expansion appears to be accelerating, an observation for which there is currently no explanation. It's usually explained by calling whatever is driving this acceleration "dark energy", but of course that doesn't really explain anything.
